notes.meaning: Paul states that he is preparing to visit Corinth for the third time. He quotes the Old Testament rule that any serious charge must be confirmed by the testimony of two or three witnesses. When he arrives, he will not act on mere rumors, but will hold a fair hearing to deal with unresolved sin.

Paul repeats the warning he gave during his second visit, speaking directly to those who had sinned earlier and have still not repented. He warns everyone that his patience has limits. If he must return to find them still practicing open disobedience, he will exercise strict discipline without holding back.

Some opponents in Corinth were demanding proof that Christ truly spoke through Paul. Paul replies that Christ is not weak when dealing with them, but has already shown His mighty power in their midst. If they continue to challenge his authority, they will experience that divine power in the form of firm correction.

Jesus appeared weak when He took on human frailty and died on the cross, yet He now lives by the power of God. In a similar way, Paul and his companions share in that outward weakness and humble suffering for Christ's sake. Even so, they share in Christ's resurrection life and will exercise God's power when serving and correcting the church.

Instead of putting Paul on trial, the Corinthians need to inspect their own hearts and conduct. They are urged to test whether their faith is genuine and whether Jesus Christ truly lives within them. If they recognize Christ at work in their own lives, it proves that the ministry that led them to Christ was real.

differ.view: Believers are called to examine their lives for evidence of true conversion, testing whether they are genuinely born again rather than merely making a false profession.
The test focuses on the quality and faithfulness of a Christian's ongoing daily walk, rather than questioning whether eternal salvation was ever received.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Believers can know that they hold the Christian faith, but they cannot have absolute certainty that they are in a state of grace or will be saved.

notes.meaning: Paul expresses confidence that honest self-examination will lead the Corinthians to see that he and his fellow workers have passed the test. Because their own church exists as the fruit of his labors, their genuine faith confirms his calling. They will know that he is a true servant of Christ.

Paul prays to God that the Corinthians will turn away from evil and do what is right. His chief concern is their moral healing, not putting on a dramatic display of his authority by punishing wrongdoers. He would gladly appear weak and unproven if it means they are walking in obedience.

Paul explains that his apostolic authority can only be used to defend and promote God's truth, never to hinder it. If the Corinthians are living in harmony with the gospel, he has no ground or desire to punish them. Church authority is given only to uphold what is right, not to harm the innocent.

Paul genuinely rejoices whenever he appears weak by having no need to exercise severe discipline, provided the Corinthians are spiritually strong. His continuous prayer is for their complete restoration. He longs to see their broken relationships mended and their church life restored to full spiritual health.

Paul writes these sharp warnings in advance so that the Corinthians will repent before his visit. By settling these problems early, he will not have to act with painful severity when he arrives. The Lord gave him authority to build up believers in faith, not to tear them down.

Paul closes his counsel with warm words, calling the believers to rejoice in the Lord. He urges them to seek harmony, encourage one another, agree in love, and live at peace. He assures them that when they pursue these things, the God of love and peace will be with them.

The believers are told to greet each other with a holy kiss, a customary sign of pure Christian affection in the ancient world. This greeting showed that past divisions were put away and mutual love was renewed. Today, believers show the same sincere Christian love through culturally appropriate greetings like a warm handshake or embrace.

The believers in Macedonia, where Paul was staying, send their warm greetings to the Corinthian church. In the New Testament, 'saints' simply means all who belong to God and are set apart for Him. This reminder linked the Corinthians with the wider family of faith across the region.

Paul ends his letter with a rich blessing naming all three Persons of the Trinity: the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. He prays that they will experience Christ's undeserved grace, the Father's unchanging love, and the close fellowship created by the Holy Spirit. He extends this blessing to every single member of the church.
